summary: Discusses using IPv6 /127 prefix lengths on point-to-point router links. Because of subnet-router anycast, one router might claim both addresses, and the document explains the problem and offers a couple of solutions, while advising that /127 be avoided between two routers. It is historic and has been replaced by RFC 6547.

eli5.summary: A tiny two-seat bench is too small if the bench itself counts as a seat that one person may grab. This says do not carve router links that tightly. The advice has since been replaced by RFC 6547.

questions: is /127 ok for ipv6 point to point links
subtitle: Why IPv6 /127 prefixes on point-to-point links cause routing conflicts.

tldr.problem: When two routers are connected by an IPv6 /127 prefix, the subnet-router anycast address feature causes one router to claim both addresses on the link, preventing the other router from using its intended address.
tldr.mechanism: A /127 subnet has only two addresses. IPv6 requires the subnet-router anycast address (with all host bits zero) to exist in every subnet. When one router adds its unicast address, it automatically adds the anycast address as well, blocking the other router's address when that router performs Duplicate Address Detection (DAD).
tldr.outcome: The document advises against using /127 prefixes on point-to-point router links and recommends /64 or /126 instead. RFC 6547 has since superseded this guidance.

today: RFC 3627 is Historic and has been superseded by RFC 6547, which provides updated guidance on IPv6 addressing for point-to-point links.

sections.title: IPv6 Addressing on Point-to-Point Links
sections.content:
Network operators traditionally use small prefix lengths for point-to-point links between routers to conserve address space. With IPv6, the smallest commonly used prefix length was /127, which allocates only two addresses. However, IPv6 requires every subnet to have a subnet-router anycast address, which is formed by setting all the host bits to zero. This mandatory feature creates a problem on /127 links.

When a router is configured with a /127 address such as 3ffe:ffff::1/127, it performs Duplicate Address Detection (DAD) on that address to ensure it is unique. The router also automatically adds the subnet-router anycast address 3ffe:ffff::0/127 to the same link. When the other router attempts to configure its planned unicast address 3ffe:ffff::0/127, DAD fails because that address is already in use as an anycast address on the first router, leaving the second router with no address.
sections.eli5: IPv6 reserves the first address in every subnet for an anycast service. On a /127 link with only two spots, that leaves just one. When the first router takes the anycast address, the second router cannot get the one remaining spot.

sections.title: The Conflict Scenario
sections.content:
Consider two routers, A and B, connected by a point-to-point link. The operator plans to use 3ffe:ffff::0/127 for Router A and 3ffe:ffff::1/127 for Router B. When Router A is configured first, it configures address 3ffe:ffff::1/127 and runs DAD to verify it is unique. The routing software automatically adds the subnet-router anycast address 3ffe:ffff::0/127 to the interface. Later, when Router B attempts to configure 3ffe:ffff::0/127 as its unicast address, DAD fails: the address is already in use by Router A as an anycast address. Router B remains without an address and cannot communicate on the link.

This problem does not occur between a router and a host (where the host is the only device needing a unicast address), but becomes critical when two routers share the link. The problem also occurs during router reboots and crashes, when addresses may be reconfigured in unpredictable order.
sections.eli5: When Router A boots up and reserves both the unicast address and the anycast address, Router B cannot get the unicast address it needs. They both fail to talk to each other.

sections.title: Addressing Solutions
sections.content:
The RFC presents several solutions. The best solution is to use /64 prefixes wherever possible, as /64 is the standard for subnets in IPv6 and avoids these issues entirely. A second option is to use only link-local addresses, which do not require global prefixes and avoid the anycast problem, though this complicates network operations like traceroute. A third solution is /126, which reserves enough addresses to avoid the anycast conflict: if the first two addresses are used as anycast and link-local, the third and fourth can be unicast addresses for the two routers. Using /126 is analogous to using /30 in IPv4 point-to-point links. The RFC notes that /120 or /112 prefixes are also reasonable alternatives.

Implementations could also be modified to never claim two addresses on a /127 link (one router claims the anycast, the other claims the unicast), but this adds complexity and creates unpredictability in which router wins the address.
sections.eli5: The best fix is to use /64 like normal. Or use /126, which has four addresses instead of two, so both routers can get what they need without fighting over seats.

sections.title: Other Long-Prefix Issues
sections.content: Beyond the /127 problem, the RFC discusses other issues with very long prefix lengths. IPv6 addressing rules define u/g bits (the 70th and 71st bits) which should be considered when assigning prefixes longer than 64 bits. Additionally, RFC 2526 reserves the last 7 bits of every non-multicast address for Mobile IPv6 Home Agent Discovery. When using long prefixes like /120, this reservation means very little address space is actually available for unicast use. The RFC recommends that implementations not perform Mobile IPv6 Home Agent Discovery on prefix lengths longer than /120.
sections.eli5: Even beyond /127, very long prefixes have other complications with special address features that were reserved for other purposes.

right.title: Router B fails to initialize
right.desc: Cannot configure 3ffe:ffff::0/127; DAD fails because Router A claims it as anycast.
